Oscar Chalupsky’s race of his life

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
SA sporting icon Oscar Chalupsky, without question one of South Africa’s most successful ever sportsmen, is currently engaged in the toughest battle of his life - a fight against bone-marrow cancer.

Unique Selling Point:
Oscar Chalupsky is a world-class padler with dozens of trophies and titles to his name. His achievements range from youngest Springbok lifesaver in 1979, South African Junior Sportsman of the Year (1981), South African bodyboarding champion ()1983) and South African Iron Man (1984) to winning the world ski paddle championships at least eight times. Also a coach, he has passed on his skills and techniques to many others in the paddle sports world. Now he is facing his biggest challenge - his battle with multiple myeloma - or more simply put, bone marrow cancer.


Summary:
Oscar Chalupsky is big on health and diet and besides a minor shoulder operation has never spent a day in hospital throughout his 40 year sporting career. But 2019 things changed for Oscar. He was racing in Australia in the World Championship when he experienced a pain in his ribs that became unbearable.

“I was in such pain. I would sleep standing up as the pain was unbearable when I tried to lie down. It was totally debilitating. And I was racing despite this constant pain and still finished,” says Chalupsky.

But in typical fashion Chalupsky was determined to not let it stand in his way. He finished 34th, at age 56, in a star-studded fleet of almost 500 paddlers in the 27km Doctor race offshore Perth.

After the race Chalupsky flew back home to Porto in Portugal. He immediately went for scans and the radiologist showed Chalupsky a tumour pressing against his spine which is the reason for the pain.

Chalupsky contacted a bone-marrow specialist in bone-marrow in Cape Town, Dr. Mike du Toit, who urged him to waste no time and fly to Cape Town immediately. Despite the unbearable pain Chalupsky was not going to cancel his wife Claire’s 60th birthday celebration on the 25th of November. “The day after she turned 60 I got onto a plane and headed for Cape Town”.

Further scans and Medical tests revealed Chalupsky had multiple myeloma - a bone-marrow cancer considered to be incurable. His cancer was at a very advanced stage and urgent treatment was needed. Months of heavy chemotherapy followed and a blood transfusion over an arduous three week period.


Further information:
Chalupsky is slowly gaining his strength back and being on a strict diet and planned exercise regime feels confident that he will not let this disease debilitate him. He has the mental power to stay positive and is confident that with the right attitude and medication he will be able to pick up his surfski again.

In July Chalupsky was nominated the winner of the 2020 Joe Glickman Award - for the greatest athlete in surfski . “It is one thing to be recognised in South Africa but receiving an award from paddlers from around the world - is very special”, says Chalupsky.

We follow the story of Chalupsky’s battle against cancer and the impact it has had on his sporting career. Support from family, fellow sportsmen and friends, have helped Chalupsky battle against his bone-marrow cancer which he is adamant he will beat.

One of the people who became a strong support for Chalupsky was Stuart Lowe, who was diagnosed with the same cancer in 2013. At the time his daughter, Jenna Lowe, was battling with a rare illness. He kept the news quiet to the family as his attention was on his daughter who eventually passed away in 2016. (A book was written about her illness “Get me to 21”.) Lowe is managing to live with the cancer and has been a strong support and mentor for Chalupsky as he could associate with the disease.

Tim Noakes, sport scientist, who has been a life-long friend of Chalupsky who has been instrumental in changing his diet which helped him to lose weight and still have energy to race. Noakes met Chalupsky when he was only 18 years in a race in Durban where Chalupsky lost his water bottle and when he finished the race, Noakes put him on the scale and said “you lost 5 kg”, to which Chalopsky replied: “Yes I lost my water bottle and had no water during the entire race”.

We interview bone-marrow specialist, Dr. Mike du Toit who will discuss the medical side of Chalupsky and his treatment. “He is very focused and has a very positive attitude,” says du Toit. There are drugs available to fight the cancer and we will continue monitoring him over the next few months to evaluate his condition,” says du Toit.

Rob Moseley, journalist and surf skier says he has learned from Chalupsky the art of tuning downward paddling and how to work with the energy of the wave instead of fighting it. They have done plenty of surfski doubles here at Miller’s Run which is a difficult race due to the swells and wind change factor of the stretch of sea between Miller’s Point and Fish Hoek. We will do his interview at Miller’s Point where he will do a shallow water surfski demonstration.

Chalupsky’s interview will be at his home in Campsbay where he will also demonstrate how he does free online surf ski lessons available on the internet. We will also do a short interview with his wife to find out how she is coping with the change it has brought in their lives. Chalupsky walks every day and we will do a short walking sequence on the promenade with Masa.
Visuals: With the help of photos and cell phone video clips we can show Chapulsky’s journey during the last 6 months in his fight against the cancer. Chalupsky has access to some of the international races and locally we will use some of the footage of Rob Mosely.

Script:


Script: Oscar Chalupsky
Duration: 8 minutes

Up sound

Oscar Chalupsky: World Class surfski paddler - when I am out there paddling there 3, 4, 5 hours I love it so much you can concentrate on what you are doing and just dream off of what you want to do. It is just you and the ocean. It is magnificent!

V/O Oscar Chalupsky is one of South Africa’s most successful water sportsmen and a world-class paddler. His achievements range from youngest Springbok Lifesaver and South African Iron man to 12 time Molokai World Surfski winner. His last win, at age 49 ended three decades of victory, making his name known around the world.

Up sound

Oscar Chalupsky: I will never forget when I won my 12th world title at age 49 I crossed that line and I just about died. But that is how far I pushed myself. I was spasming, I could not breath, it was like I was dying.

V/O At seven Chalupsky started paddling with his father Paul - a veteran Springbok canoeist. Coached by his father, he became the youngest winner of the gruelling 244 km Port Elizabeth to East London race at age 18. Professor Tim Noakes was a young sports science researcher at the time.

Prof. Tim Noakes: Exercise Scientist: My friendship began in 1982 when I was researching the Texan Challenge, and the night before the race started, Oscar got up and said: “Listen guys I just want to warn you, you are all paddling for second place. I am going to win this race,” and this is an 18 year old and then I realised he is something different.

V/O Over the next three decades Chalupsky became a legend in surfski communities, coaching paddlers across the globe.

Up sound

V/O Rob Mousley met Chalupsky in 2005 at one of the Miller’s Run races in False Bay.

Rob Mousley: Friend of Oscar - Perhaps the most important lesson I have learnt from him is to be immersed in the moment. So when you are out there on those big waves is to catch a wave and then stay with it. I have had times out there that I cannot believe how little effort he is putting in and yet we are going so fast. Because he is using the energy of the moving wave.

V/O Chalupsky is known to work outside his comfort zone. But in November last year he started experiencing an unbearable pain during a race in Perth, Australia. It brought his life to a standstill.

Oscar Chalupsky: And I said: “Jee this pain is something else,'' and I can’t believe that someone can endure this sort of pain. And I thought the only time I would get relief is by doing things, so I was running and I was paddling and I felt good. As soon as I lay down I was in trouble. I could not even sit down.

V/O Chalupsky flew home to Portugal - rushing to the home he’d been sharing with his wife Claire in Porto for five years. A scan revealed a tumour on his spine.

Oscar Chalupsky: And that is when they gave me the news: you have between 4 - 6 months to live. And you think ok, tumour, how bad can it be and when you start phoning around, I have a lot of people in the medical field and they all said, no, that is just the secondary one you have got something else going on in your body. And that is where it started.

Masa Kekana: And when you heard the grim news, weren’t you a little bit scared?

Oscar Chalupsky: It was shocking to me because I have been so fit for so long and Claire took it harder than me. I probably cried a little bit but Claire was worse and then obviously the kids.

Masa Kekana: Claire, how did you feel when you heard the news?

Claire Chalupsky - It’s so terrible to hear that. It is just so ghastly and we both just burst into tears at the time. And then it just became adapting and getting use to that news.

V/O The news came the day before Claire’s 60th birthday. Chalupsky was determined to go ahead with the family birthday celebrations.

Oscar Chalupsky: And she said no. And I said excuse me whether it is 6 months, 4 months whatever, still we are here and I am feeling fine and let’s have a good party on your 60th birthday.

V/O Chalupsky flew to South Africa shortly after to consult with specialists in Cape Town. Several tests at UCT’s medical hospital and Constantiaberg clinic confirmed Chalupsky’s condition: bone-marrow cancer or myeloma. He was referred to Dr. Mike du Toit.

Dr Mike du Toit - Clinical Haematologist - He had this back pain and the back pain was due to damage to one of the vertebrae in his spine, the lower thoracic region and that has become compromised and that was really where the pain was coming from.

V/O Over the next three months Chalupsky received chemotherapy and a gruelling bone marrow transplant. This was one race Chalupsky was not prepared for and needed support from someone who had been on this journey before. He was introduced to Stuart Lowe.

Stuart Lowe: Multiple Myeloma patient - A mutual friend contacted me and said why don't you have a cup of coffee with Oscar and I described what I knew about the drug challenges and trying to get medication for Multiple Myeloma and describing the journey that Oscar is going to have to go through.

Oscar Chalupsky: I got to know him and he gave me a lot of help with what I was going to go through and it was nice. I talk of support and that is where you need these guys.

Up sound

Oscar Chalupsky: The bone marrow transplant, a lot of people told you how tough it is but nobody can really explain it till you have done it. So it was really tough and my wife and my family, when I was talking to them on Whatsapp they were crying because they could see you have no power. And a person like me having no power, is like this can’t happen to me.

Up sound

V/O But Chalupsky remained positive and used social media to encourage others to speak out about their experiences.

Oscar Chalupsky: You have to live your life and every time I put out a facebook page there are so many people that struggling through these times, it gives them hope.

V/O After three months of gruelling medical treatment Chalupsky was finally home with Claire, eating healthily, and slowly regaining his strength.

Oscar Chalupsky: And funnily enough just out there I walked, first just 800 meters. and I would just lie on this couch for the whole afternoon recovering from 800 meters. I am used to 80km paddle.

Up sound

V/O Chalupsky’s enduring commitment to coaching has not gone unnoticed. In July he received the Joe Glickman Lifetime Achievement Award for his unfailing contribution and commitment in the sport of surfski paddling presented to Chalupsky online.

UP audio...The first recipient of the Joe Glickman award should be none other than Mr. Oscar Chalupsky…

V/O Joe Glickman was a world renowned sports journalist and paddler who followed Chalupsky’s career closely. He raced in several surfski doubles with Chalupsky before he died of cancer in 2015.

Up audio Oscar:…”I really appreciate it. Surfski is my life”

V/O In spite of cancer, Chalupsky believes he will be back in the surfski again: coaching and helping fellow sportsmen.

Dr. Mike du Toit: The disease itself is not considered a curable condition as yet. Generally it is something you would aim to control as long as possible. There are a lot of new drugs coming out for people with myeloma, unfortunately they are extremely costly so we tend to keep them for more advanced situations.

V/O Chalupsky has offered to help raise funds for Multiple Myeloma patients who can’t afford the expensive treatment.

Stuart Lowe. Oscar and myself and a group have formed a patient advisory board for patients with Multiple Myeloma and are lobbying and are having great success with the help of ‘campaigning for cancer’ in bringing the stakeholders together.

Oscar Chalupsky: There is no better thing in life than to save another person’s life and as a lifesaver I was doing that since I was 8 or 9 years old.

V/O Chalypsky’s mind has always been stronger than his body and he is determined to face this immense challenge head-on with the trademark courage that has defined his sporting career.

Oscar Chalupsky: At the end of the day it is how you approach and how you handle the adversity in life. Because there is no cure for this multiple myeloma the only way I thought of life is I am going to live long enough so that they can find a cure and I am sure they will.

Promo 2: With the trademark courage and commitment that has defined his sports career, Oscar Chalupsky is determined to face a cancer without a known cure head-on.

Promo 3: With sporting fans across the globe rallying for ‘Team Oscar,’ champion sports star Oscar Chalupsky is facing the biggest challenge in his life - fighting a cancer without a known cure.

And a person like me having no power, is like this can’t happen to me. Up sound V/O But Chalupsky remained positive and used social media to encourage others to speak out about their experiences. Oscar Chalupsky: You have to live your life and every time I put out a facebook page there are so many people that struggling through these times, it gives them hope. V/O After three months of gruelling medical treatment Chalupsky was finally home with Claire, eating healthily, and slowly regaining his strength. Oscar Chalupsky: And funnily enough just out there I walked, first just 800 meters. and I would just lie on this couch for the whole afternoon recovering from 800 meters. I am used to 80km paddle. Up sound V/O Chalupsky’s enduring commitment to coaching has not gone unnoticed. In July he received the Joe Glickman Lifetime Achievement Award for his unfailing contribution and commitment in the sport of surfski paddling presented to Chalupsky online. UP audio...The first recipient of the Joe Glickman award should be none other than Mr. Oscar Chalupsky… V/O Joe Glickman was a world renowned sports journalist and paddler who followed Chalupsky’s career closely. He raced in several surfski doubles with Chalupsky before he died of cancer in 2015. Up audio Oscar:…”I really appreciate it. Surfski is my life” V/O In spite of cancer, Chalupsky believes he will be back in the surfski again: coaching and helping fellow sportsmen. Dr. Mike du Toit: The disease itself is not considered a curable condition as yet. Generally it is something you would aim to control as long as possible. There are a lot of new drugs coming out for people with myeloma, unfortunately they are extremely costly so we tend to keep them for more advanced situations. V/O Chalupsky has offered to help raise funds for Multiple Myeloma patients who can’t afford the expensive treatment. Stuart Lowe. Oscar and myself and a group have formed a patient advisory board for patients with Multiple Myeloma and are lobbying and are having great success with the help of ‘campaigning for cancer’ in bringing the stakeholders together. Oscar Chalupsky: There is no better thing in life than to save another person’s life and as a lifesaver I was doing that since I was 8 or 9 years old. V/O Chalypsky’s mind has always been stronger than his body and he is determined to face this immense challenge head-on with the trademark courage that has defined his sporting career. Oscar Chalupsky: At the end of the day it is how you approach and how you handle the adversity in life. Because there is no cure for this multiple myeloma the only way I thought of life is I am going to live long enough so that they can find a cure and I am sure they will. _____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promos 1: Oscar Chalupsky, undoubtedly South Africa’s greatest watersport champion, is facing the biggest challenge in his life - a fight against a cancer without a known cure. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): SA sporting icon Oscar Chalupsky, without question one of South Africa’s most successful ever sportsmen, is currently engaged in the toughest battle of his life - a fight against bone-marrow cancer.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Oscar Chalupsky is a world-class padler with dozens of trophies and titles to his name. His achievements range from youngest Springbok lifesaver in 1979, South African Junior Sportsman of the Year (1981), South African bodyboarding champion ()1983) and South African Iron Man (1984) to winning the world ski paddle championships at least eight times. Also a coach, he has passed on his skills and techniques to many others in the paddle sports world. Now he is facing his biggest challenge - his battle with multiple myeloma - or more simply put, bone marrow cancer.
metadata.Summary: Oscar Chalupsky is big on health and diet and besides a minor shoulder operation has never spent a day in hospital throughout his 40 year sporting career. But 2019 things changed for Oscar. He was racing in Australia in the World Championship when he experienced a pain in his ribs that became unbearable. “I was in such pain. I would sleep standing up as the pain was unbearable when I tried to lie down. It was totally debilitating. And I was racing despite this constant pain and still finished,” says Chalupsky. But in typical fashion Chalupsky was determined to not let it stand in his way. He finished 34th, at age 56, in a star-studded fleet of almost 500 paddlers in the 27km Doctor race offshore Perth. After the race Chalupsky flew back home to Porto in Portugal. He immediately went for scans and the radiologist showed Chalupsky a tumour pressing against his spine which is the reason for the pain. Chalupsky contacted a bone-marrow specialist in bone-marrow in Cape Town, Dr. Mike du Toit, who urged him to waste no time and fly to Cape Town immediately. Despite the unbearable pain Chalupsky was not going to cancel his wife Claire’s 60th birthday celebration on the 25th of November. “The day after she turned 60 I got onto a plane and headed for Cape Town”. Further scans and Medical tests revealed Chalupsky had multiple myeloma - a bone-marrow cancer considered to be incurable. His cancer was at a very advanced stage and urgent treatment was needed. Months of heavy chemotherapy followed and a blood transfusion over an arduous three week period.
metadata.Further information: Chalupsky is slowly gaining his strength back and being on a strict diet and planned exercise regime feels confident that he will not let this disease debilitate him. He has the mental power to stay positive and is confident that with the right attitude and medication he will be able to pick up his surfski again. In July Chalupsky was nominated the winner of the 2020 Joe Glickman Award - for the greatest athlete in surfski . “It is one thing to be recognised in South Africa but receiving an award from paddlers from around the world - is very special”, says Chalupsky. We follow the story of Chalupsky’s battle against cancer and the impact it has had on his sporting career. Support from family, fellow sportsmen and friends, have helped Chalupsky battle against his bone-marrow cancer which he is adamant he will beat. One of the people who became a strong support for Chalupsky was Stuart Lowe, who was diagnosed with the same cancer in 2013. At the time his daughter, Jenna Lowe, was battling with a rare illness. He kept the news quiet to the family as his attention was on his daughter who eventually passed away in 2016. (A book was written about her illness “Get me to 21”.) Lowe is managing to live with the cancer and has been a strong support and mentor for Chalupsky as he could associate with the disease. Tim Noakes, sport scientist, who has been a life-long friend of Chalupsky who has been instrumental in changing his diet which helped him to lose weight and still have energy to race. Noakes met Chalupsky when he was only 18 years in a race in Durban where Chalupsky lost his water bottle and when he finished the race, Noakes put him on the scale and said “you lost 5 kg”, to which Chalopsky replied: “Yes I lost my water bottle and had no water during the entire race”. We interview bone-marrow specialist, Dr. Mike du Toit who will discuss the medical side of Chalupsky and his treatment. “He is very focused and has a very positive attitude,” says du Toit. There are drugs available to fight the cancer and we will continue monitoring him over the next few months to evaluate his condition,” says du Toit. Rob Moseley, journalist and surf skier says he has learned from Chalupsky the art of tuning downward paddling and how to work with the energy of the wave instead of fighting it. They have done plenty of surfski doubles here at Miller’s Run which is a difficult race due to the swells and wind change factor of the stretch of sea between Miller’s Point and Fish Hoek. We will do his interview at Miller’s Point where he will do a shallow water surfski demonstration. Chalupsky’s interview will be at his home in Campsbay where he will also demonstrate how he does free online surf ski lessons available on the internet. We will also do a short interview with his wife to find out how she is coping with the change it has brought in their lives. Chalupsky walks every day and we will do a short walking sequence on the promenade with Masa. Visuals: With the help of photos and cell phone video clips we can show Chapulsky’s journey during the last 6 months in his fight against the cancer. Chalupsky has access to some of the international races and locally we will use some of the footage of Rob Mosely.
